responses:
# Work — Living Summary

**Where things stand:** Jordan is three days from a new manager (Priya, starting the 21st, on legacy marketing pages — widely understood at Meridian to be the holding pen for people the company hasn't gotten around to letting go of) and eleven days from an onsite interview at Northlight, a four-person design team hiring fast, ideally by October. The lease got renewed on the 14th regardless — a year, $150 more, through next October — a decision made deliberately independent of how Northlight turns out.

**How it got here:** The thread starts July 30th with Marcus announcing "team realignment" in standup — reorg number two in Jordan's 14 months at Meridian. Lena, exhausted by her third reorg in two years, started looking immediately. Through August, Marcus put Jordan through whiplash feedback cycles on the internal dashboard — "doesn't align with the direction" on the 3rd, then "too safe" on the 11th on the exact revision he'd asked for — each round triggering a shutdown pattern Jordan named explicitly: bad news at work, withdrawal, isolation, eventually forcing out to Groundwork coffee shop where work on a personal project (Coda, a music practice app) restored some sense of competence. Lena left the team on the 14th, and the news that her offer came through hit harder than Jordan expected, since she was the one person who made bad meetings bearable. On the 20th, a dashboard iteration finally landed — "this is the right direction" — but by the 24th the reorg specifics arrived: Jordan's role marked "under evaluation," delivered by Marcus with total flatness. On September 1st the resolution came: not cut, but moved to legacy marketing under Priya, which Jordan and everyone else recognized as being parked rather than valued. Lena, by then at Northlight, pushed a referral through anyway, texted the submission through on September 9th. Jordan's portfolio update — dreaded since July — turned out to be mostly done already, anchored by an honest, unflattering case study about Coda's free-play feature (built as a "trophy case," used by a friend as a bug tracker instead — a mismatch Jordan hadn't seen despite nine days of daily use). The phone screen with Ana on the 11th went well; onsite scheduled for the 24th.

**The throughline Jordan keeps naming:** every work blow triggers the same shutdown — blinds down, phone off, isolate — and every recovery has come through someone else refusing to let the impression of "fine" hold: Mika showing up unannounced, Dev getting told the truth instead of an excuse, Mom getting the real story at Greenwood Park instead of another five weeks of blackout, Lena insisting on the referral over Jordan's reflexive self-disqualification. Jordan has flagged, as of September 14th, that the situation didn't actually improve — the reorg still landed badly — but the pattern of hiding it did, and that this, not the job outcome, is what changed.

**Open threads:** the Northlight onsite on the 24th and whether an offer follows; the awkwardness of three days under a brand-new manager before taking a personal day to interview elsewhere; whether Coda keeps being the thing that saves Jordan on bad weeks once (if) the job stops being the source of the bad weeks; and the recurring office-emptying dream, which found stairs for the first time on the most recent pass.

# Dating — Jordan

**Where things stand:** Jordan is a few weeks into something with Dev, a session musician/bass teacher, and it's tentatively good. Lunch is planned for Saturday (8/29). As of 8/27, they've just cleared a small but meaningful hurdle: Jordan told Dev the truth about a canceled plan instead of hiding behind an excuse, and Dev responded with warmth instead of judgment.

**How it got here:** It started 8/8 with a nervous coffee-and-walk date at Greenwood Park — shirt changed twice, Mika talked Jordan out of bailing beforehand. The date went well: easy silences, a shared bench (previously occupied with an ex, Mikayla), and Dev getting genuinely interested in Coda, Jordan's practice-tracking app project, asking sharp questions about it unprompted. Jordan left calmer than they'd felt in weeks and consciously tried not to over-label the feeling.

Second date, 8/15, dinner at a Thai place — more of the same chemistry, Dev playing an unfinished song off their phone, real conversation about Coda that turned into actual feature design (the "free play" mode idea came out of this dinner). Dev texted a bass cover afterward with no context. Jordan's guard was visibly lowering.

The complication: on 8/11, a sprint review went badly (Marcus's contradictory feedback, Lena's sympathetic look), and Jordan responded with the withdrawal pattern — canceled dinner with Mika, sat in the dark, didn't engage even with Pepper. Jordan named the pattern explicitly in that entry: work criticism triggers retraction, and recognizing it doesn't stop it.

That same pattern hit Dev on Monday before 8/27 — Jordan canceled with a fake "swamped" excuse rather than admitting the real reason. On 8/27, Jordan chose to go back and tell Dev the truth: bad news at work, shutdown, not about them. Took four drafts to send. Dev's response — "I would rather know you're having a bad week than think you didn't want to see me," plus the disclosure that Dev does their own version of disappearing (into the bass) — landed hard. Jordan felt disproportionately lighter afterward.

Jordan also drew an explicit comparison to Mika, who Jordan says "got around this years ago by refusing to believe" Jordan's deflections — implying Mika has never taken the "I'm fine" excuse at face value. Dev doesn't have that history yet, so Jordan named the choice plainly: if Dev is going to be let into this part of Jordan's life, Jordan has to hand over the truth voluntarily rather than counting on someone else to see through the cover story.

**Open threads:** Lunch with Dev on Saturday (8/29) — first hangout since the honesty exchange. Whether Jordan can keep choosing disclosure over the "fine" performance when the next work blow-up happens (and there will be one, given the sprint review pattern). Whether Dev becomes someone who gets read into the withdrawal cycle the way Mika is, or whether this repeats the cancel-and-hide pattern. Nothing yet on where Mikayla fits historically beyond the bench detail — an ex who isn't otherwise discussed.

# Health — Jordan

**Where things stand:** Jordan is in a noticeably better place than a month ago, though the underlying pattern hasn't disappeared, just stopped having the last word. Running remains the steadiest form of self-care — mostly solo now at Greenwood Park, working up to the hill trail extension, legs burning, clear head. Sleep has been rockier: a recurring dream about an empty, flickering office with no way out has shown up three times, most recently the night of 9/14, though this time — for the first time — Jordan found the stairs and walked out instead of hitting a dead end. Jordan's not claiming the dream means anything causal, but notes it.

**How it got here:** The thread starts 7/30 with news of a Q4 team restructuring, landing on top of an already rough 14 months (this would be Jordan's second reorg). The response was the familiar one: staying late to avoid the feeling, low appetite, cereal for dinner. A run with Mika the next day (7/31) offered real relief, and Mika's observation — that Coda is the actual portfolio, that Jordan feels better whenever they work on it — became a recurring theme other people (Lena included) later echoed.

Early August brought a bad stretch tied directly to Marcus's whiplash feedback at work: 8/3 (design review torn apart, shutdown, no dinner, two hours alone in the dark, Pepper curled against him) and 8/11 (same pattern — cancelled on Mika, sat on the floor without lights, recognized the withdrawal in real time and still couldn't stop it). Jordan named the mechanism explicitly both times: criticism or feeling unseen triggers a retreat inward, a refusal to reach out even to the person who'd help most, something closer to punishing himself for caring than actual coping.

8/14 was a hinge point: the office dream first appeared (woke at 4am, early run to cope), and later that same day Lena told Jordan she's leaving the company in three weeks. Jordan was glad for her and also registered it as one more anchor lifting — she's the person who debriefs the bad meetings with him.

8/19's solo run cleared the fog enough to make the lease decision (unrelated logistics, health-adjacent as a stress relief valve). By 9/11, a strong phone screen with Northlight's Ana shifted the whole emotional register — Jordan ran afterward specifically to burn off adrenaline, and noted on the hill trail that the external situation hadn't changed but suddenly felt lighter because a door had opened.

By 9/14, signing the lease, Jordan explicitly connects the improvement not to the job resolving (it didn't — he's still stuck reporting to a new manager, Priya, starting 9/21) but to a behavioral shift: telling people the truth instead of disappearing. Dev, Mom, Lena all got let in on hard things in the preceding weeks. Jordan names the old pattern directly — "I don't want help, I want to disappear" — and says it's still true in the moment, just no longer decisive.

**Open threads:** Whether the withdrawal pattern holds up under the next real blow (the onsite is 9/24, three days after a brand-new manager starts). Whether the office dream stays resolved or recurs a fourth time. Whether Coda keeps functioning as the reliable mood-lifter it's been. No mention yet of sleep hygiene, therapy, or medication — this seems to be Jordan self-tracking a mood/withdrawal cycle without outside intervention so far.

# Jordan — Creative Thread

**Current state:** Coda, Jordan's side-project practice-tracking app for musicians, has gone from a months-long noodle to the centerpiece of a real job search. As of September 9th, Jordan wrote up the case study properly for the first time — including the honest, slightly embarrassing part — and submitted it with a Northlight application via Lena's referral. The phone screen with Ana on September 11th went well; an onsite is coming in about two weeks. Meanwhile the app itself keeps evolving through real use, not just Jordan's own.

**How it got here:** The pattern started small — July 28th, two hours at Groundwork on the practice log screen, streak counters with little flame animations. What crystallized over the following weeks was a cycle Jordan named outright on August 12th: bad thing happens at work → shut down → isolate → eventually get to Groundwork → build something → feel human again. Mika named it first, on July 31st, calling Coda "the portfolio update" before Jordan believed her. The building continued through the reorg anxiety of early August — the metronome (8/4), quick-start cards (8/12) — each session a way of processing the Marcus situation sideways.

Dev entered the picture August 8th and became a real collaborator, not just a listener: their offhand question about tracking "unstructured practice" (8/15) became the free-play mode, sketched on a napkin, built in an hour and a half on August 25th after weeks of Jordan circling the problem. On September 3rd, Dev actually used it — and revealed that Jordan had built a "trophy case" (a feature for collecting evidence you're okay) when Dev needed a "bug tracker" (a tool for triaging toward a deadline). Jordan wrote this up with unusual clarity: nine days of daily use, and still couldn't see it, because Jordan was the wrong user.

Alongside the coding, music came back in its own right. Mika signed them both up for an open mic without asking; Jordan practiced "Fast Car" at home with Pepper howling along (8/17), then actually performed it at The Lantern on August 21st, shaky but real, with Dev and Mika both there. That night became a marker — the three of them together, easy and warm.

Lena's departure (8/14) and eventual referral (9/9) threaded through all of this — she was the second person to say "Coda could be the thing," and the case study that got written was, by Jordan's own account, the strongest piece in the portfolio, built at a coffee shop specifically to feel better on bad days.

**Open threads:** The onsite at Northlight is coming, full day, four interviews plus a design presentation. Whether Coda becomes an actual exit from Meridian — or just the thing that made the exit possible — isn't settled. The free-play mode's redesign (making marks neutral, letting review assign meaning) hasn't been built yet. Dev has a gig on the 19th using Coda-logged practice. And whatever this thing is with Dev — still unlabeled, deliberately so — keeps showing up at the edges of the music and the app both.

# Jordan — Social

Right now the core of Jordan's social world is a small, steady set of people doing a lot of load-bearing work: Mika, Dev, and until this month, Lena. The pattern that's defined the last several weeks — bad news at work knocks Jordan flat, someone shows up (or Jordan drags themselves out) and the gears start turning again — is still the operating system, but there are signs the middle part is getting shorter, and the cast has widened from "Mika alone" to something more like an actual group.

Mika has been the anchor throughout. She's the one who noticed back on 7/31 that Coda might *be* the portfolio, who talked Jordan out of cancelling on Dev (8/8), who showed up with pad thai after the restructuring news without asking questions (8/24), and who's stopped believing Jordan's excuses years ago — a habit Jordan leaned on again when reflecting (8/27) on having fed Dev a fake excuse instead. She also set the open mic in motion by signing Jordan up before they could object (8/17), which led to the 8/21 night at The Lantern: a shaky but real performance of "Fast Car," Dev and Mika meeting for the first time and hitting it off immediately over an obscure documentary, and the three of them staying two hours after. Jordan named that night as something they want to keep happening.

Dev entered the picture on 8/8 — a walk at Greenwood Park, an easy quiet, an offhand mention of Coda that turned into real interest. Since then the relationship has deepened past "new friend": Jordan cancelled a lunch with a fake excuse during the 8/24 spiral, then on 8/27 chose to tell Dev the truth instead, and Dev's response ("I disappear too, I just do it with a bass in my hands") landed as its own small turning point — a first sign that Dev might become someone Jordan can be honest with by default, the way Mika already is. They have lunch planned for that Saturday. On 9/3, Dev came over and actually used Coda's free-play mode, which turned into a real working session between them — Dev finding practice gaps the app wasn't built to surface, Jordan realizing how differently the two of them use the tool. It was collaborative and unglamorous in a way that felt like an actual friendship doing actual things together, not just company.

Lena was the office half of this support system — the look across the table during a bad meeting, the "you crushed it" text after the 8/20 demo. Her last day was 8/28; she pushed back hard on Jordan's reflexive "I'm not good enough" when she offered to put Jordan's name in at Northlight, and followed up on 9/1 the moment the reorg news landed ("that's the holding pen and you know it... hang on"). Her absence from the floor is already registering as a loss separate from the reorg itself.

Threads still open: whether the Northlight referral goes anywhere once Lena's settled in; what happens with Dev now that honesty is on the table between them; whether Mika and Dev's rapport becomes a regular three-person thing or stays occasional; another open mic Mika's already angling to plan; and whether the shortening "middle part" of Jordan's crash-and-recover cycle holds up under the next real hit, given the legacy marketing move lands on the 21st.

# Family — Jordan

Mom and Dad are in the picture mostly through Mom right now, who's the one calling, visiting, noticing things. As of early September, the big event was Mom's Labor Day weekend visit, and the thing sitting freshest is Jordan's own pattern of not telling her things until much later than makes sense.

It started on 8/7, when Mom called to plan a Labor Day visit and Jordan spent the call not mentioning the work situation (the reorg, the role under evaluation) so she wouldn't worry. The call itself was ordinary — Dad's knees, Mom's book club, a neighbor's dog getting into her garden — the kind of update that comes with every call. Jordan told her things were "good," which felt technically true but was really a way of keeping her out of it.

The days after were spent quietly bracing for the visit — cleaning, submitting a maintenance request for a ceiling stain that never got fixed (8/9), avoiding the lease renewal decision. None of this touched the family thread directly except as the backdrop Jordan was scrambling to tidy before Mom saw it.

Mom arrived Friday night of Labor Day weekend and stayed through Sunday (9/6). She did the apartment tour, complimented the green rug, and had brought a folding chair from home because Jordan had mentioned back in July only owning two — the kind of thing she just remembers and acts on without being asked. She also brought a box of Dad's old guitar picks, cleaned out of the garage, with the message that "he wanted you to have them." Dad doesn't play anymore because of arthritis in his hands.

The bigger moment came Saturday, walking the loop at Greenwood Park. Jordan finally told her everything about work — the restructuring, the role evaluation, Lena leaving — five weeks after first knowing. Mom's response wasn't anger, just sadness: "I wish you'd told me in July." She said Jordan could tell her anything, then asked a string of sharp follow-up questions, including one that landed harder than expected — what Jordan would be doing if the job weren't taking up so much mental space. Saturday night Jordan made roasted chicken, Mom ate at the folding card table without a single comment on it, and Pepper — who usually hides from guests — slept on her lap for an hour.

Mom left Sunday afternoon. Jordan noticed the apartment felt very quiet afterward and sat with the recognition that this is a repeated move: running an information blackout on people who would actually help — naming Mika, Dev, and now Mom as the same pattern playing out again.

Open threads: whether Jordan tells Mom about the lease decision (renewal was due September 15, still unresolved as of these entries) or about how the work situation eventually resolves. Whether the "I wish you'd told me in July" conversation actually changes the pattern next time something hard comes up, or whether it repeats again. Dad remains mostly offstage — knees, arthritis, the guitar he no longer plays — known through Mom rather than directly.

# Pets

Pepper, Jordan's cat, has been a fixture through a rough stretch — the one steady presence across a summer of work turmoil, a lease decision, and a slow habit of finally telling people things.

The thread starts small in late July, with Pepper waiting by the door doing her sit-on-the-shoes thing (7/28), forgiving Jordan instantly for a night spent working at Groundwork. From there she shows up as a kind of emotional barometer. On bad days — the reorg news (7/30), the brutal design review (8/3), the "role under evaluation" gut-punch (8/24) — she does something specific: sleeps on Jordan's chest, climbs into their lap and purrs hard enough to feel it, or just sits there while Jordan can't bring themselves to pet her back. Jordan has noted outright that she only sleeps on their chest when they're down, and that she "knows."

The lighter, more comic side of the record: knocking a water glass off the nightstand at 2am (8/1), claiming the new green rug the day it arrived with a proprietary slow roll, sitting on the forbidden kitchen counter during Mom's phone call (8/7) and again while Jordan made soup (8/9) — an unspoken truce where she breaks the rule and Jordan pretends not to notice. There's the open mic prep on 8/17, where Pepper sat on the guitar amp and howled along during the quiet verse of "Fast Car," which made Jordan laugh hard enough to lose the chord progression. And on 8/19, she batted at shoelaces while Jordan worked out the lease math on the living room rug.

A stranger note came on 8/14: a recurring dream about an empty, wrong office, and Jordan woke from it to find Pepper staring from the foot of the bed — the timing making the dream feel more ominous in the retelling. That dream recurred on 9/14, but this time Jordan found the stairs and got out, which they flagged as maybe meaning nothing, maybe not.

On 9/3, Pepper played a small supporting role in the Coda testing session with Dev — leaving the room at the slapped bass notes and returning right as Dev nailed the phrase clean, which Jordan read as her rendering a verdict.

The biggest new development is Mom's visit over Labor Day (9/6): Pepper, who usually hides from guests, slept on Mom's lap for a full hour — notable enough that Jordan wrote it down as a small, plain fact among the heavier stuff about the five-week information blackout on the work situation.

Most recently, on 9/14, the night Jordan signed the lease renewal, Pepper was found asleep on the green rug with her white feet curled up — the entry's closing image, low-key and settled, against a lot of unresolved churn (the Northlight interview on the 24th, a new manager starting the 21st).

Open thread: no vet visits, no health scares, no other animals in the picture — just Pepper, aging alongside Jordan's year, apparently still the most reliable read on how Jordan's actually doing whenever Jordan won't say it directly.

# Jordan — Emotional Throughline

**Where things stand:** Jordan is in an unusually open, unguarded stretch. After a summer of getting knocked down repeatedly by work and withdrawing into a familiar dark-apartment-blinds-down pattern, something shifted around late August: the recovery time started shrinking, and Jordan began actually telling people the truth in real time instead of after the fact. The lease is signed (renewing at Jordan's apartment, $150 more, through next October), a Northlight onsite is scheduled for the 24th, and the withdrawal cycle — while still present — is being caught faster and interrupted more often by Jordan's own hand rather than requiring Mika to show up at the door.

**How it got here:** The engine of the summer was Meridian's slow-motion reorg. It surfaced July 30, metastasized through a string of Marcus's whiplash feedback (Aug 3, Aug 11), and produced a recognizable spiral: criticism or dismissal at work → shutdown → isolation → eventually Groundwork, where building something on Coda pulled Jordan back to feeling human. Jordan named this pattern explicitly multiple times (Aug 12, Aug 24) without being able to break it — until Sept 1, when the actual bad news landed (moved to "legacy marketing," the holding pen) and the dark-couch phase lasted twenty minutes instead of a full day.

Two people kept surfacing as the ones who pull Jordan out: Mika, who invited Jordan into an open mic performance (Aug 21) that became a real high point, and who shows up with food and no questions; and Lena, whose July 30 warning and Aug 14 departure announcement removed Jordan's main workplace ally but also became the catalyst for real momentum — she referred Jordan to Northlight (Sept 9) and pushed back hard against Jordan's reflexive "I don't think I'd be good enough" (Aug 28), a self-doubt Jordan recognized as automatic rather than sincerely held.

Dev entered as a steadying, non-anxious presence (Aug 8 walk, Aug 15 dinner) and became the person Jordan chose to practice honesty with — canceling with a fake excuse on Aug 24, then circling back Aug 27 to tell the real version, which Dev met with reassurance rather than judgment. That exchange seemed to crack something open: Jordan named the core mechanism directly — that protecting the appearance of being fine is what makes the withdrawal last, and that undoing it requires *handing the heavy thing to someone* rather than hiding it. Jordan noticed the same pattern with Mom, having run a five-week blackout on the whole reorg situation until her Sept 6 visit, when she said, simply, that she wished she'd known sooner.

Coda itself, the side project, quietly became the throughline rather than a distraction from one — first as a coping mechanism, then (via Mika and Lena separately telling Jordan the same thing) as the actual centerpiece of the portfolio that got Jordan the Northlight interview. The recurring dream about the empty, exit-less office building appeared three times across the summer; the last version, after signing the lease, ended with Jordan finding the stairs.

**Open threads:** The Northlight onsite is the 24th. Priya starts managing Jordan on the 21st — three days before that interview. Whether Coda ships anywhere beyond Dev's phone is unresolved. And whether Jordan's new instinct to hand people the heavy thing holds under real pressure, or reverts once the immediate crisis (job, Lena leaving, the reorg) resolves one way or another, is still unproven.

Jordan's still in the same one-bedroom, and as of September 14 the lease is signed for another year — $150 more a month, through next October 31st. The decision came together slowly over August: a lease renewal notice sat unopened for weeks, then got resolved mid-run at Greenwood Park on the 19th, when Jordan walked through the math (moving costs vs. staying) and realized the neighborhood — Groundwork three blocks away, the park a ten-minute jog — is home now. Signed it a day before the September 15 deadline, from a window table at Groundwork, cortado going cold.

The apartment itself has its known flaws: a bedroom door that doesn't close all the way, a ceiling stain from an upstairs leak maintenance never actually fixed despite a photo submitted August 9 (predictably, nothing happened), and a card table doing duty as a dining table. Small quality-of-life wins this stretch: a deep green rug bought August 1 that Pepper immediately claimed and that Mom later said "really warms it up" — same thing Jordan thought when buying it. Domestic rhythms are steady — cleaning on Sundays, a rotation of roasted chicken thighs and white bean kale soup, Pepper knocking things off nightstands at 2am and colonizing the forbidden kitchen counter by unspoken treaty.

The bigger thread of the month was Mom's Labor Day weekend visit (planned as of the August 7 call, happened around September 6). Jordan cleaned for three hours, the ceiling stain remained defiantly unfixed, and Mom brought an unprompted folding chair from her trunk and a box of Dad's old guitar picks he can't use anymore because of his arthritis. The visit became the occasion for Jordan finally telling Mom about the work situation — the restructuring, the role under evaluation, Lena leaving — during a walk around Greenwood Park's pond, after having deliberately kept her in the dark since July specifically to spare her worry. Mom's response ("I wish you'd told me in July," not angry, just sad) landed hard; Jordan named the pattern of information blackouts as something done repeatedly to Mika, Dev, and Mom alike. Pepper, who normally hides from guests, slept on Mom's lap for an hour — noted as its own small event.

By the September 14 entry, the lease decision sits inside a larger reckoning: Jordan chose not to let an unresolved job situation (the Northlight interview looming on the 24th, a new manager starting the 21st) dictate housing, reasoning that if the commute changes later, a car is affordable with the prospective raise. The throughline Jordan draws is that home stayed steady while everything else wobbled — not because the job resolved, but because Jordan started telling people the truth instead of disappearing into it.

Open threads: the ceiling stain, still unfixed. Whether the Northlight job will eventually force a rethink of the commute or a car. And whether the pattern — going quiet on the people closest before finally cracking open — repeats again next time something heavy shows up.
